title: China carrier blanks post-Golden Week: capacity stays tight
metaDescription: Carriers blank 39 sailings through early November. Teu-mile demand drops for the first time since January. Your Q4 bookings just got harder.
bottomLine: Carriers have blanked 39 sailings between 5 October and 8 November across the three main east-west trades, cutting capacity by 5% at the exact moment Chinese factories reopen and export volumes gear up. Teu-mile demand fell for the first time since January, driven by Golden Week blanks, newbuild deliveries, and more ships shifting back to Suez. If you have stock ready in the next two weeks, expect allocation games and premium pricing.

stories.headline: Carriers blank 39 sailings through November despite factory restart
stories.tldr: Thirty-nine sailings cancelled between 5 October and 8 November on transpacific, transatlantic and Asia-Europe routes, cutting capacity 5%.
stories.whatHappened:
Carriers have announced 39 blanked sailings across the three main east-west trades from Week 41 (5 to 11 October) through Week 45 (2 to 8 November), according to Drewry's Cancelled Sailings tracker. The blanks cover transpacific, transatlantic and Asia-Europe routes.

The capacity reduction amounts to 5% across those trades during a period when Chinese factories reopen after Golden Week and container flows typically accelerate. Golden Week began on 1 October and factories were closed through the holiday.

Several long-haul services have been cancelled in response to weaker Chinese export volumes during the week-long holiday, according to container shipping consultancy Linerlytica.
stories.whyItMatters:
You are trying to book space out of China right now, or you will be in the next ten days. The blanks mean less capacity at the moment demand picks up again. Carriers have already removed 5% of available slots, and they control which bookings go on which ships.

If your stock is ready to ship this week or next, you will compete for fewer boxes with everyone else whose factory just reopened. Carriers will allocate space to their contract customers first, then fill remaining slots at higher spot rates. You either pay the premium or you wait for the next sailing, which pushes your delivery date back a week or more.

The timing matters for Q4. A week's delay now compounds through your inbound lead time, your FBA receiving window, and your ability to restock before peak demand. If you are selling anything with a November or December sales curve, a blanked sailing in mid-October can cost you the high-margin weeks.
stories.hotTake: Carriers are protecting rates, not responding to actual demand. They know factories are reopening and volumes will surge, but they would rather run fewer ships at higher utilisation than compete for cargo at lower prices. If you wait for spot rates to drop, you will wait through Q4.
actions: Check your booked sailings in Weeks 41 to 45 and confirm the vessel name has not changed
Move any ready stock to the port this week rather than waiting for a consolidation window
Lock contract space now for shipments in the second half of October, even if the rate is higher than you want

stories.headline: Teu-mile demand falls for first time since January
stories.tldr: Container shipping teu-mile demand declined for the first time since January, hit by Golden Week blanks, newbuild deliveries and Suez shifts.
stories.whatHappened:
Teu-mile demand growth regressed for the first time since January, according to container shipping consultancy Linerlytica. The decline reflects a combination of blanked sailings by major carriers during China's Golden Week, increased newbuild vessel deliveries, and more ships returning to the Suez Canal on Asia-Europe routes.

Golden Week began on 1 October and factories were closed through the holiday. Several long-haul services were cancelled in response to weaker Chinese export volumes during that period.

More ships have shifted back to Suez Canal routing on Asia-Europe lanes, which shortens voyage distances and reduces teu-miles even if the same number of containers move.
stories.whyItMatters:
Teu-mile demand is the clearest measure of how much work the container shipping system is actually doing. When it falls, carriers have more capacity than cargo, and that should mean lower rates. But the number fell because carriers blanked sailings and ships switched to shorter routes, not because your demand disappeared.

You still need to move the same volume of goods. The capacity just got redistributed in a way that benefits carriers, not shippers. Shorter Suez routes mean faster transits and lower carrier fuel costs, but you do not see those savings in your freight rate. Carriers pocket the efficiency gain and use the blanked sailings to keep spot rates from collapsing.

The first teu-mile decline in nine months signals that the post-pandemic demand surge has ended, but it does not mean cheap freight is coming back. Carrier discipline is tighter than it was in 2019, and they will blank more capacity before they let rates fall far enough to hurt contract renewals.
stories.hotTake: Teu-mile demand is falling but your rate is not, which tells you everything about who has pricing power. Carriers have learned to manage capacity faster than demand can shift, and they will keep that edge until someone breaks ranks. No one is breaking ranks.
actions: Stop waiting for a spot rate collapse that is not coming and lock in the rate you have now
Model your Q4 freight budget at current spot rates rather than assuming a seasonal drop
If you are on a Suez-routed service, confirm your transit time has actually shortened and adjust your FBA send-in dates

stories.headline: Philippine patrol plane intercepted by Chinese J-16 fighter over Scarborough Shoal
stories.tldr: Chinese J-16 fighter made unsafe close approaches to Philippine C-208 patrol aircraft near Scarborough Shoal on Saturday, AFP says.
stories.whatHappened:
A Chinese J-16 jet fighter made repeated unsafe close approaches to a Philippine C-208 light patrol aircraft near Scarborough Shoal on Saturday, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines. The Philippine plane was conducting a routine patrol flight when two Chinese military aircraft approached.

One of the Chinese planes moved in too close for safe operation, including manoeuvres in front and behind the Philippine aircraft, the AFP said. The C-208 is a small, unarmed prop plane used for maritime patrols. The Shenyang J-16 is a fourth-generation strike fighter derived from the Soviet-era Su-27.

The AFP called it part of a recurring pattern of unsafe and coercive behaviour against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations. The C-208 aircrew completed the mission and returned to base without incident. China's Southern Theater Command said in a statement on Monday that PLA aircraft took action to expel a Philippine aircraft that illegally intruded into territorial airspace over Scarborough Shoal.
stories.whyItMatters:
You are shipping goods through the South China Sea and the Philippine Sea on every Asia-Europe and transpacific route. Scarborough Shoal sits 600 miles southeast of the Chinese mainland and west of Luzon, in waters that both sides claim. Air and naval incidents in contested zones do not close shipping lanes, but they raise insurance premiums and add political risk to your transit time.

If tensions escalate, carriers reroute around contested areas or add war risk surcharges. Those surcharges show up on your invoice without warning, and they do not come off when the news cycle moves on. The AFP said this is part of a recurring pattern, which means it will happen again and carriers will price that risk into your rate.

The incident also signals that China will continue to enforce its territorial claims in the South China Sea regardless of international rulings. The Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled in 2016 that China's claims in the Philippine EEZ have no basis in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. China refused to recognise the ruling and has expanded its presence. Your shipping lane runs through the middle of that dispute.
stories.hotTake: This does not change your routing this week, but it adds another layer of risk to every sailing through the South China Sea. Carriers price in conflict risk faster than you can budget for it, and the surcharge stays on your invoice long after the headline fades.
actions: Review your ocean freight contract for war risk and security surcharge clauses and confirm the trigger conditions
Ask your forwarder if any carriers have rerouted Asia-Europe or transpacific services in the past month due to South China Sea incidents
Budget for a 2 to 5% surcharge buffer on sea freight rates for Q4 and Q1 in case tensions escalate further

faq.question: Why are carriers blanking sailings when Chinese factories just reopened?
faq.answer: Carriers blank sailings to protect rates, not to match demand. Thirty-nine sailings cancelled between 5 October and 8 November cut capacity by 5%. Factories reopen after Golden Week and export volumes typically surge, but carriers run fewer ships at higher utilisation rather than let spot rates fall. They allocate space to contract customers first and fill remaining slots at premium spot rates.

faq.question: What does teu-mile demand mean and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Teu-mile demand measures total container shipping system work: containers multiplied by distance travelled. It fell for the first time since January, driven by Golden Week blanks, newbuild deliveries and ships shifting to shorter Suez routes. A falling number usually signals overcapacity and lower rates, but this decline came from carriers cutting sailings and shortening routes, not weak shipper demand.

faq.question: Should I wait for ocean freight rates to drop in Q4?
faq.answer: No. Carriers blanked 39 sailings through early November and teu-mile demand fell for the first time in nine months, but spot rates are not collapsing. Carrier discipline is tighter than before the pandemic. They will blank more capacity before they let rates fall enough to hurt contract renewals. Lock in the rate you have now and move your stock.

faq.question: How do I get space on a ship if carriers are blanking sailings?
faq.answer: Move stock to the port as soon as it is ready rather than waiting for consolidation. Check booked sailings in Weeks 41 to 45 and confirm the vessel name has not changed, because carriers reassign bookings when they blank a sailing. Lock contract space now for shipments in the second half of October, even if the rate is higher than you want.

faq.question: Does the South China Sea incident affect my shipment?
faq.answer: Not immediately. A Chinese J-16 fighter made unsafe close approaches to a Philippine patrol plane near Scarborough Shoal on Saturday. The AFP called it part of a recurring pattern. Air and naval incidents do not close shipping lanes, but they raise insurance premiums and add war risk surcharges to your freight invoice without warning. Those surcharges stay on long after the news fades.
